quote: Every now and then, another neuroscience press release appears, claiming that, because researchers used an f MRI to spot the brain doing something-or-other during a decision process, it’s not you who chooses, it’s your brain.
content: The essay is right, and the subsequent science strengthened its point. The press releases were reporting Libet’s readiness-potential experiments (Libet et al. (1983)) and the imaging study that decoded left-versus-right button choices from prefrontal activity up to ten seconds before the reported decision, at about sixty per cent accuracy (Soon et al. (2008)). The inference that “the brain decided before you did” assumed the readiness potential was a decision; a later model showed that it is what one sees by averaging spontaneous fluctuations time-locked to a threshold crossing, so that the “decision” it precedes is largely the timing of an arbitrary act, and the preceding buildup is noise that happened to cross (Schurger, Sitt & Dehaene (2012)). The essay’s point stands on its own logic and now on the data as well: the fMRI results are about the causal structure of a decision within physics, which is where the essay locates the chooser.

quote: My position might perhaps be called “Requiredism.” When agency, choice, control, and moral responsibility are cashed out in a sensible way, they require determinism—at least some patches of determinism within the universe.
content: The position has a name and it is older than the word “compatibilism.” Hume’s Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), §VIII, argues that liberty not only is compatible with necessity but requires it: actions that were not caused by the agent’s character and motives would be “entirely loose and separate” from the agent and could not be attributed to them, and “it is impossible to admit of the one without the other.” Hobbes said the same in the Leviathan, Schlick restated it in 1930, and Dennett’s Elbow Room (1984) is a book-length version with the essay’s own emphasis on control requiring lawful mechanism. The essay presents this as a departure from compatibilism; it is compatibilism’s classical form, and the definition it gives of compatibilism (“free will can be intuitively and satisfyingly defined” so as to fit determinism) is not one a compatibilist would recognize, since the thesis is about what freedom consists in, not about definitions. The point the essay makes is a good one and it has been made, in nearly these words, for two hundred and sixty years. The stack trace the homework asked for is not attempted; what the essay supplies is the answer to the question it said was not the assignment.
